entry.title: How an Embedded SoC Boots, Part 2: Signed Boot Images and the Secure Enclave

link.title: How an Embedded SoC Boots, Part 2: Signed Boot Images and the Secure Enclave

entry.content:
TL;DR: Secure boot is a chain of trust: every stage checks the next one’s signature before it jumps to it, starting from code and keys that can’t be changed. On the i.MX95 the roots are NXP’s key inside the secure enclave’s ROM and a hash of your public keys burned into fuses. The boot image, flash.bin, is a row of signed containers: NXP’s enclave firmware first, then your M33 firmware and SPL, then TF-A and U-Boot, which SPL loads and checks later. Until you close the part, failed checks are only logged.

Where part 1 left off

Part 1 followed the boot from power-on to the moment the boot ROM finds a valid image header on the boot device. This post is about what the ROM does next: how it decides whether to trust the image, what the image looks like inside, and where its pieces end up.

Part Topic
1 From power to the first instruction: PMIC, reset, BootROM
2 Signed boot images and the secure enclave (this post)
3 Waking up the DRAM: initialization and training
4 The system controller firmware and SCMI
5 SPL → TF-A → OP-TEE → U-Boot: exception levels and hand-offs
6 Linux takes over, plus a “last console line → failed stage” cheat sheet

As before, the ideas are general and the i.MX95 is the worked example. The details come from NXP’s imx-mkimage source, the AHAB documentation and code in NXP’s U-Boot, and the i.MX95 reference manual.

Why a boot image needs a signature

A boot ROM could check an image with a checksum or a hash. That catches a corrupted flash, but not an attacker: anyone who can change the image can also fix up its hash. To decide whether an image is authentic, the device needs public-key cryptography. You sign the image offline with a private key that never leaves your build server, and the device verifies the signature with the matching public key.

Each stage has to check the next before it jumps to it, because once untrusted code runs, it can do anything the stage before it could. That gives a chain of trust: the ROM checks the first bootloader, the bootloader checks the next one, and so on up to the kernel. The first link has to be something an attacker can’t change, and on a SoC that means code in mask ROM.

Every vendor builds the same chain in its own way. Older NXP parts (i.MX6, i.MX7, i.MX8M) use HAB; the i.MX8, i.MX8X, i.MX8ULP and i.MX9 families use AHAB, where a separate security subsystem does the checking. Arm’s Trusted Firmware-A has its own trusted boot scheme based on X.509 certificates. The rest of this post uses AHAB on the i.MX95, but the questions are the same everywhere: where are the keys, what is signed, and who checks what.

The root of trust: ROM code and a key hash in fuses

The ROM needs a public key it can trust, and the obvious place to keep it is in fuses. Fuses are expensive, though, and a public key is large. So most designs burn only a hash of the public keys. The keys themselves travel inside the boot image, and the ROM accepts them only if their hash matches the fuses. Swapping in your own keys doesn’t help an attacker, because the hash won’t match.

AHAB works this way. You generate up to four Super Root Keys (SRKs) with NXP’s Code Signing Tool. Their public halves go into an SRK table inside every signed container, and the SHA-256 hash of that table goes into the SoC’s 256-bit SRK_HASH fuses. Having four keys means one can be revoked if it leaks, without changing the fuses.

The i.MX95 has a second root: NXP’s own public key, built into the EdgeLock Secure Enclave (ELE) ROM. It is used for one thing, checking the ELE firmware that NXP signs and ships. So there are two roots of trust on the chip, NXP’s and yours.

The last piece is the lifecycle, a state kept in fuses that says how strict the chip should be:

  • OEM open: the ELE runs every check and records failures as events, but boots the image anyway. Every development board is in this state, and it is how you test a signed image without risking the board.
  • OEM closed: a failed check stops the image. You move a part here with U-Boot’s ahab_close command once a signed image boots cleanly, and there is no way back.

U-Boot’s ahab_status command shows both: on an i.MX95 it prints Lifecycle: 0x00000010, OEM Open (or 0x00000040, OEM closed), followed by any events the ELE has recorded.

Containers: what is actually signed

A signed boot image needs more than a signature appended to a binary. The ROM has to know which images are inside, where each one goes in memory, which core runs it, and which bytes the signature covers. AHAB puts all of that into a container:

  • A header with a tag, version and length, some flags, two version numbers and an image count.
  • An image table, one entry per image: its offset in the file, its size, its load address and entry point, flags (image type, target core, hash algorithm) and a hash of the image. imx-mkimage uses SHA-384 by default.
  • A signature block with the SRK table, the signature, and an optional certificate for a subordinate signing key, so the SRKs themselves can stay offline.

The signature covers the header, the image table and the SRK table, but not the images. They are covered through their hashes in the signed table. That keeps the expensive signature check to one small block per container. The images are only hashed, and the ELE can check each one as it is loaded.

The two version numbers serve different purposes. fuse_version is the anti-rollback counter: the ELE refuses a container whose fuse_version is lower than a counter in fuses, so you can retire an old, vulnerable image by burning that counter forward. sw_version is a software version number that tools and the boot flow can use.

What’s inside the i.MX95 flash.bin

Here is the image from part 1, opened up. It holds three containers, and the boot ROM only reads the first two.

Container 1: the ELE firmware. NXP builds and signs it, and you include it unchanged from NXP’s firmware package. It is specific to the silicon revision: mx95a0-ahab-container.img for A0 and mx95b0-ahab-container.img for B0. This is the revision trap from part 1’s debug table.

Container 2: your M33 firmware and SPL. In NXP’s BSP build (with the OEI enabled) it holds:

Image Load address Runs on
OEI (one or two, depending on the silicon revision) 0x1FFC0000 (M33 TCM) M33
System Manager 0x1FFC0000 (M33 TCM) M33
SPL 0x20480000 (OCRAM) A55

The OEI and the System Manager have the same load address on purpose. The ROM loads the OEI and runs it, the OEI trains the DRAM and returns (part 3), and then the System Manager overwrites it. Configurations with M7 firmware add an M7 image to the same container.

The container headers sit back to back at the start of the file, at offset 0 and 0x400, and the images follow. Some configurations add a third header at 0x800, for V2X firmware or a placeholder for it.

Container 3: TF-A, U-Boot and optionally OP-TEE. imx-mkimage builds it separately as u-boot-atf-container.img and appends it to flash.bin at the next 1 KiB boundary. The boot ROM never reads it. SPL does, after the OEI has trained the DRAM: TF-A goes to 0x8A200000 and U-Boot to 0x90200000 in NXP’s defaults.

How SPL handles container 3 matters for security. It copies the header into memory, asks the ELE to authenticate it, and from then on uses only that checked copy. Each image is then loaded and checked against its hash before SPL jumps to TF-A. All of this lives in U-Boot’s CONFIG_AHAB_BOOT code. Without that option, SPL loads container 3 without checking it, and the chain ends at SPL.

There are two ways to build this image:

  • NXP’s BSP uses imx-mkimage. You copy the firmware, SPL, U-Boot and TF-A into iMX95/ and run a target such as make SOC=iMX95 REV=B0 OEI=YES flash_a55. Each target is a single mkimage call that lists the images, the target cores and the load addresses.
  • Upstream U-Boot builds flash.bin itself with binman, using the nxp-imx9image entry type. You copy the same firmware files into the U-Boot tree and run make, as the U-Boot i.MX95 EVK documentation describes. The result has the same container layout.

Following the chain of trust

Pick a scenario in the figure below to see what happens when a check passes, and when it fails on an open and on a closed part.

The roles split cleanly. The M33 boot ROM reads the containers and loads the images, but makes no trust decisions itself. The ELE makes every decision: its ROM checks the ELE firmware with NXP’s key, and its firmware checks container 2 for the boot ROM and container 3 for SPL with your keys. Past U-Boot, the ELE is out of the picture: U-Boot checks the kernel itself, with a signed FIT image, or asks the ELE to check an OS container. That link is part 6.

Signing in practice

A full signing walkthrough is longer than this post, and NXP’s AHAB guides in the U-Boot source cover it step by step. This is the order of operations, and why each step comes where it does:

  1. Generate the keys with the Code Signing Tool’s ahab_pki_tree.sh, and the SRK table and its hash with srktool. Keep the private keys somewhere safer than the build machine, such as an HSM or an offline machine.
  2. Sign container 3 first. It is built on its own (make SOC=iMX95 u-boot-atf-container.img), signed with cst, and copied back under the same name, because flash.bin is assembled from that file.
  3. Build flash.bin and sign container 2. mkimage prints the container and signature block offsets, and the CST input file (the CSF) needs them.
  4. Burn the SRK hash with U-Boot’s fuse prog on the fuse words for your part. An error here leaves you with a part that can never boot a signed image, so check the values twice.
  5. Boot the signed image on the still-open part and run ahab_status. It must say No Events Found!.
  6. Close the part with ahab_close, only after step 5 is clean.

Closing is irreversible. On a closed part, every image has to be signed with keys that match the fuses, including images you load over USB serial download. A wrong SRK hash or a missing signature on a closed part leaves the board unable to boot.

What this means when you debug a real board

Symptom Look at first
Image is read, then the boot ROM moves to its next boot stage ELE container for the wrong silicon revision, or on a closed part, a container that fails its check
Board boots, ahab_status lists events Unsigned container, wrong keys, or an SRK hash that doesn’t match the fuses. Harmless on an open part, fatal once closed
SPL starts, U-Boot never does Container 3 missing or at the wrong offset, DRAM not trained, or container 3 failing its check with CONFIG_AHAB_BOOT
Signed image boots on one board, not on another Different lifecycle or SRK fuses between the boards; compare their ahab_status output
Board boots with an unsigned image you expected it to refuse The part is still OEM open

The last row is the one to remember. On an open part, signing mistakes don’t stop anything, so they are easy to miss until the day the part is closed. Make ahab_status part of your test before you close the first production board.

What’s next

Container 2 has been checked and its first image, the OEI, is about to run on the M33. Part 3 follows it: what it takes to bring up LPDDR5, what the training firmware does, and why the DRAM can’t be used until it is done.

Sources

  • nxp-imx/imx-mkimage, iMX95/soc.mak and src/imx8qxb0.c: container targets, load addresses, the container 3 alignment, container and signature block fields, the default hash algorithm
  • nxp-imx/uboot-imx: doc/imx/ahab/introduction_ahab.txt and doc/imx/ahab/guides/mx8ulp_9x_secure_boot.txt (AHAB concepts, the i.MX95 image layout, signing and fusing steps, ahab_close); arch/arm/mach-imx/ele_ahab.c (ahab_status, lifecycle values, container 3 authentication); common/spl/spl_imx_container.c (SPL loading container 3)
  • U-Boot documentation: i.MX95 EVK and arch/arm/dts/imx95-u-boot.dtsi in upstream U-Boot: firmware files per silicon revision, the binman build
  • NXP, i.MX 95 Applications Processor Reference Manual, “System Boot” chapter (available from NXP with an account): image container sets, ROM image validation through the ELE ROM, the boot flow after a validation error
  • NXP, Code Signing Tool (CST) and its AHAB user guide, available from NXP with an account: key generation and container signing
entry.summary: The second post in a series on how a modern embedded SoC boots. How the boot ROM decides whether to trust an image, what a signed boot container looks like, and what is inside the i.MX95's flash.bin.

entry.title: How an Embedded SoC Boots, Part 1: From Power to the First Instruction

link.title: How an Embedded SoC Boots, Part 1: From Power to the First Instruction

entry.content:
TL;DR: On a modern embedded SoC, the first instruction does not run on the application cores. The PMIC brings up the power rails in a fixed order and releases reset, then a BootROM starts on a small boot core. It works only from on-chip memory, reads the boot pins and fuses, brings up the boot device and reads the first image, which holds the firmware for the secure enclave. None of this prints to a console, so debugging this stage means knowing what to measure.

About this series

Most embedded Linux engineers know the boot flow as “U-Boot, then the kernel”. On a modern SoC, several pieces of firmware run before U-Boot proper, often on more than one processor, and a dead board can fail in any of them. This series follows the boot from power-on to Linux PID 1, one stage per post, with an animated diagram for each stage.

Part Topic
1 From power to the first instruction: PMIC, reset, BootROM (this post)
2 Signed boot images and the secure enclave
3 Waking up the DRAM: initialization and training
4 The system controller firmware and SCMI
5 SPL → TF-A → OP-TEE → U-Boot: exception levels and hand-offs
6 Linux takes over, plus a “last console line → failed stage” cheat sheet

The ideas apply to most modern application processors. For concrete examples I use NXP’s i.MX95 on a generic board with LPDDR5, an SD card slot and eMMC, because it has every stage: a separate boot core, a secure enclave and a system controller. Other SoCs name and split these stages differently, and the exact pins, fuses and offsets always differ, so check your part’s datasheet and reference manual for those.

Which core boots first

A modern application processor has more than one kind of core. On the i.MX95:

Processor Role
Cortex-M33 Boot core and system controller
Cortex-A55 cluster Application cores: SPL, TF-A, U-Boot, Linux
Cortex-M7 Optional real-time core, for your own firmware
EdgeLock Secure Enclave (ELE) Separate security subsystem: keys, fuses, signature checks

The boot core is the M33, not the A55. It runs three pieces of firmware in turn:

  1. The BootROM, in mask ROM. It picks the boot device and loads the first images.
  2. The OEI (Optional Executable Image), which initializes the DRAM and returns to the ROM (part 3). NXP also uses OEIs for other early setup, such as TCM initialization, and the set of OEI images differs between A0 and B0 silicon.
  3. The System Manager, which owns power, clocks and resets and serves the application cores over SCMI (part 4).

On the i.MX95, the firmware that owns the hardware runs on the small core that boots first, and the big application cores start later, as its clients. Several recent SoCs use a similar split, but it isn’t universal: some put the system controller on a dedicated microcontroller that isn’t the boot core, and many simply boot on an application core. Older i.MX parts are an example of the last kind. On the i.MX8M, for example, the ROM runs on the first Cortex-A53 core and the Cortex-M core is an optional extra. Which core runs the ROM is the first thing to find out for any new SoC, because it tells you where to look when nothing happens.

Before the first instruction: power

Nothing runs until the power rails are up. A PMIC (power management IC) generates the board’s rails from the input supply. Its OTP (one-time-programmable memory) holds the power-up sequence: which rails turn on, in which order, at what voltage and with what delay. NXP’s reference power design for the i.MX95 splits this between two parts: a PF09 PMIC, which sequences the board and supplies most of the rails, and PF53 regulators for the high-current VDD_SOC and VDD_ARM rails (AN14910). NXP’s 19 × 19 EVK follows it: its block diagram shows one PF09 and two PF53s, fed from the 12 V adapter through two FS5600 converters. The FRDM i.MX 95 Pro board does the same on a smaller scale, with a PF09 plus a PF5302 for VDD_SOC. Which PF53 feeds which rail on the EVK is in its schematic, not the block diagram. Other boards may use other PMICs; the principle is the same.

The order matters. Powering one domain before another can drive current through protection diodes into an unpowered domain, or leave a block in an undefined state. Every SoC datasheet specifies its own power-up sequence. The i.MX95’s, simplified, goes like this, and other SoCs follow a similar pattern with different details:

  1. The always-on domain (the battery-backed BBSM supply) comes up first and goes down last.
  2. The core logic rails: VDD_SOC for the SoC logic, and VDD_ARM for the A55 cluster.
  3. The 0.8 V analog, PLL and PHY supplies, and then the 1.8 V supplies.
  4. The SoC’s DRAM interface rails, VDD2H_DDR and then VDDQ_DDR. The memory chip has its own rails (VDD1, VDD2H, VDD2L, VDDQ) and its own power-up order, defined by the LPDDR5 standard (JESD209-5) and the memory datasheet. Its 1.8 V VDD1 comes up first, so it usually shares the 1.8 V step above. The PMIC sequence has to satisfy both the SoC and the memory.
  5. The 3.3 V I/O, and the SD card’s switchable I/O supply.
  6. Reset release: the power-on reset input, POR_B, is held asserted for the whole sequence and released once every rail is in regulation. On NXP’s reference designs the PMIC drives it; a board can also use a separate supervisor.

The core voltage isn’t one fixed number. The i.MX95 datasheet lists different VDD_SOC values for different drive modes, so the value you measure depends on the part, the PMIC configuration and the firmware. Compare it with your schematic, not with another board.

When POR_B is released, the SoC latches its boot-mode pins. Changing the boot switches after this has no effect until the next power-on reset.

From here on, the DRAM is powered but unusable. It holds nothing, and the DDR controller can’t talk to it reliably until it has been initialized and the link trained, which happens later (part 3). Until then, all code and data live in on-chip memory.

The BootROM

The BootROM is mask ROM inside the SoC. It is fixed in silicon and can’t be updated; fuses can only adjust what it does. Out of reset, the boot core fetches its first instruction from it. On the i.MX95 the A55 cluster and the M7 stay in reset, while the ELE starts its own ROM in parallel (more below).

The ROM’s world is small:

  • Code runs from ROM.
  • Working memory is on-chip RAM. On the i.MX95 the ROM keeps its own stack and data in a reserved part of the M33’s tightly coupled memory (TCM). The images it loads go to the load addresses given in the image headers: the M33 firmware into the TCM, the A55’s SPL into the general-purpose on-chip RAM (OCRAM). DRAM is off limits until it has been initialized.
  • It prints nothing. The i.MX95’s ROM doesn’t use a UART at all (the reference manual’s list of hardware the ROM uses has none). Many other BootROMs are silent too, but not all, so check your part. On the i.MX95, the first console output comes from later firmware, and only if it was built with a console enabled.

Which console prints first depends on the BSP:

Stage Console on the i.MX95 Prints when
BootROM none never
OEI, System Manager M33 debug UART when built with debug output, or by default
SPL, TF-A, OP-TEE, U-Boot, Linux A55 console UART depends on each one’s console configuration

On a board with a debug USB port, several UARTs often come out of one USB-serial chip. Find out which one belongs to which core before you decide a board is dead: on the i.MX95 the earliest output, if any, comes from the OEI or the System Manager on the M33 UART, not on the Linux console.

At the same time, the secure enclave (the ELE on the i.MX95) comes out of reset and runs its own internal ROM. The two ROMs work together: the M33 ROM fetches images from the boot device, and the ELE ROM handles secure boot, starting with the NXP-signed ELE firmware in the first container. Once that firmware runs, the ELE also provides runtime services (key storage, crypto, fuse access) to the later stages. The boot image holds more than the ELE firmware: a second container carries the OEI, the System Manager, the A55 bootloader and optional M7 firmware. Loading and authenticating the first container is the last step of this post and the start of part 2.

Step through the whole sequence below. The timeline at the bottom shows the rails and POR_B coming up; it is simplified and not to scale.

Boot modes

The ROM’s first decision is where to boot from. It has two inputs:

  • Boot-mode pins, latched at reset. They are often shared with other functions, so the board has to hold them at the right levels while reset is asserted.
  • Boot fuses, which select the boot device and its parameters (bus width, speed, controller instance) and can lock the configuration down.

Most SoCs combine them into three kinds of boot mode:

  1. Boot from fuses. The fuses alone select the boot device. This is the normal setting for production hardware, because a stray switch setting can’t change it.
  2. Normal boot. The pins select the device directly: eMMC, SD, or SPI flash. Convenient during development.
  3. Serial download. The ROM skips the boot media and waits for an image over USB.

The pin encodings differ between parts, even within one family, and how the pins reach a switch is a board decision. NXP’s i.MX95 EVK has a four-position switch; the smaller FRDM board brings out only two of the pins. Always take the switch settings from your board’s documentation, never from another board or another SoC.

When the selected device has no valid image, many ROMs try other sources before giving up. The i.MX95 reference manual documents this order:

  1. The primary image set on the primary boot device: SD, eMMC, FlexSPI NOR or SPI NAND.
  2. A secondary image set on the same device, at an offset set by fuses, if those fuses are programmed.
  3. A recovery device: a serial NOR flash or EEPROM on LPSPI1 or LPSPI2, only if a fuse enables recovery.
  4. USB serial download, on USB1 (some parts use USB2 instead), unless a fuse disables it.

Between stages, the i.MX95 ROM records the next stage in a reset-controller register and resets the SoC. So I’d expect a board with no valid image to access its boot device, reset, try again, and eventually enumerate on USB; I haven’t captured this on a scope myself. On a secured product with serial download disabled, a board with no valid image just stops. Which stages are active depends on the fuses, so the exact behaviour differs between boards, and NXP’s documentation is per silicon revision.

Boot devices: where the ROM reads

Once the device is chosen, the ROM brings up its controller and reads the first image header at a fixed location. That location differs per device type:

Device Where the image starts (i.MX95) Why
SD card 32 KiB from the start of the card fixed by the ROM; clears the partition table
eMMC offset 0 of a boot hardware partition the boot partitions sit outside the user area
SPI NOR after a small configuration block for the chip the ROM needs to learn how to drive this flash chip

The offsets themselves are fixed by each SoC’s ROM, but the reasoning behind them carries over:

  • SD: 32 KiB is where the i.MX95 ROM looks; it’s part of the documented boot-image layout, not something you choose. A useful side effect is that the image doesn’t collide with the partition table: a GPT with the usual 128 entries fills the first 17 KiB of the card. The offset differs between families: the i.MX6 and i.MX7 read the image at 1 KiB, which clashes with a GPT; the i.MX8MQ and i.MX8MM use 33 KiB; the i.MX8MN, i.MX8MP, i.MX8QXP and i.MX93 use 32 KiB, like the i.MX95. The first real partition starts well after the boot image, often at a few MiB. Writing the image is a single dd:

    sudo dd if=flash.bin of=/dev/sdX bs=1k seek=32 conv=fsync

    Forgetting seek=32 is the classic mistake: it overwrites the partition table and leaves the ROM nothing to find.

  • eMMC: an eMMC has two boot partitions (boot0, boot1) and a user area, all separate hardware areas. A setting in the eMMC itself (PARTITION_CONFIG, set with mmc partconf in U-Boot) selects which one it boots from. The bootloader usually goes in the selected boot partition, often boot0, where nothing else lives and it survives a reflash of the user area. The i.MX95 ROM can also boot from the user area, at 32 KiB like SD.
  • SPI NOR: flash chips differ in commands, dummy cycles and maximum clock. The ROM starts in a slow mode that every chip supports, reads a configuration block from a known offset, then reconfigures the controller and reads the image. On the i.MX95 this is the FlexSPI Configuration Block (FCB), with the read settings for that flash chip. imx-mkimage’s FlexSPI target (make flash_a55_flexspi) generates it and places it at 1 KiB, before the image at 4 KiB. So a NOR image is a separate build. You can’t write the SD image to NOR and expect it to boot.

On SD, the SD specification requires the host to identify the card with a clock of 400 kHz or less. Then it raises the clock according to what the card and controller support. That slow start is the first thing to look for with a scope on the SD clock line.

Pick a device in the figure below, then step through what the ROM does with it, including the fallback paths when there is no valid image:

The header check is shallow on purpose: the ROM checks that an image is there before it trusts anything inside it. The signature checks come next, through the secure enclave, and are the subject of part 2.

Serial download

Serial download is how you recover a board with an empty or broken boot device. Select it with the boot switches rather than waiting for the ROM to fall back to it: that skips the failed attempts and works even if fallback is configured differently.

Each vendor has its own USB protocol and host tool for this. On the i.MX95, the ROM shows up on the host as a USB HID device with NXP’s vendor ID 1fc9, and NXP’s uuu (Universal Update Utility) talks to it:

# Linux host: install udev rules once, so uuu doesn't need root
uuu -udev | sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/70-uuu.rules
sudo udevadm control --reload
sudo udevadm trigger   # or replug the board

# Is the ROM waiting?
lsusb | grep -i 1fc9

# Boot flash.bin into RAM, without writing anything
uuu flash.bin

# Write flash.bin to the eMMC boot partition
uuu -b emmc flash.bin

# Show what a built-in script really does on your uuu version
uuu -bshow emmc

The first command loads the bootloader into RAM over USB and changes nothing on the board’s storage, which makes it the quickest way to test a new flash.bin. -b selects one of uuu’s built-in scripts. The emmc script boots the same image, then uses fastboot in the running U-Boot to write it to the eMMC boot partition and select that partition with mmc partconf. That needs a U-Boot with fastboot support, which NXP’s BSP builds have. A related script, emmc_all, also writes a full disk image (for example a Yocto .wic) to the eMMC user area. The scripts and the U-Boot side change between uuu and BSP releases, so check yours with uuu -bshow.

What this means when you debug a real board

Most of what this post covers happens before the A55 console is up. On the i.MX95 nothing in this post prints: the ROM is silent, and the earliest possible output comes from the OEI or the System Manager on the M33 UART, and only if they were built with debug output. A silent board can be stuck anywhere from the PMIC to the secure enclave firmware, so work from the bottom up and measure instead of guessing:

Symptom Look at first
One or more rails missing or wrong PMIC configuration, a fault the PMIC latched, a shorted rail. Measure every rail and read the PMIC fault registers
Rails fine, reset stays asserted A rail just outside its power-good window, a supervisor holding reset, a missing pull-up on the reset line
Reset released, boot device never accessed Boot switches (latched at reset), boot fuses, power to the boot device; check whether the board enumerates on USB
Boot device read, then USB enumeration No valid image: wrong offset, blank media, or an image built for another board or boot device
Board in serial download doesn’t appear on the host Wrong USB port, a charge-only cable, USB supply problems, or serial download disabled by fuse
Image is read, nothing ever prints A later stage failing with its debug output off, or a signature failure on a closed (secured) part

Signature failures don’t always stop the boot. On a part whose lifecycle is still OEM open, which covers most development boards, the ELE logs authentication failures of your own images and boots them anyway. Only an OEM-closed part refuses them. The ELE firmware itself is different: it is NXP-signed and always checked.

That makes the wrong silicon revision a trap on new parts, because firmware images can be revision-specific. The U-Boot documentation for the i.MX95 EVK lists separate ELE firmware containers for A0 and B0 silicon, and an image built for one doesn’t boot on the other. I expect that to look like the “no valid image” row above, with the ROM falling back to serial download, but I haven’t tested it on a board. Check the marking on the chip against what you built.

Two habits save time at this stage. First, keep a known-good SD card around: if it boots, the hardware up to the ROM is fine, and the problem is in your image. Second, when you bring up a new board, scope the rails and the reset line once at power-on and save the trace. When a later board revision fails to boot, you have something to compare against.

What’s next

The ROM has found a valid image header and handed the secure enclave its firmware. Part 2 opens the image: how signed boot images are structured, what the enclave checks and with which keys, how the chain of trust continues, and how the i.MX95’s flash.bin is put together.

Sources

  • U-Boot documentation: i.MX95 EVK: firmware files, silicon revisions, the SD dd command
  • NXP, i.MX 95 Applications Processors Data Sheet for Industrial Products: power-up sequence, operating voltages, boot modes
  • NXP, i.MX 95 Applications Processor Reference Manual, “System Boot” chapter (available from NXP with an account): boot stages and fallback, ROM memory use, image offsets, ELE ROM, recovery and serial download devices
  • NXP, i.MX 95 19 × 19 mm EVK block diagram: PF09, 2× PF53 and FS5600 power parts, boot devices
  • NXP, PF09 product page, AN14910 PF09 PMIC Hardware Design Guidelines and UM12527 FRDM-IMX95-PRO Board User Manual: PF09/PF53 power architecture
  • NXP, Getting Started with the i.MX 95 19 mm × 19 mm EVK and Getting Started with FRDM-IMX95: boot switches, debug UARTs
  • nxp-imx/imx-mkimage, nxp-imx/imx-oei, nxp-imx/imx-sm: the boot image and the M33 firmware (parts 2–4)
  • nxp-imx/mfgtools (uuu): USB IDs and the built-in emmc and emmc_all scripts
  • JEDEC, JESD209-5: Low Power Double Data Rate 5 (LPDDR5), and your memory vendor’s datasheet: DRAM rails and power-up sequence
  • SD Association, Physical Layer Simplified Specification: card identification at ≤ 400 kHz
  • UEFI Forum, UEFI Specification, GPT chapter: partition table size and location
entry.summary: The first post in a series on how a modern embedded SoC boots, from power-on to Linux PID 1. What happens before any console output, from power sequencing and reset to the BootROM choosing a boot device.

entry.title: Cameras on i.MX95, Part 1: From Photons to /dev/video

link.title: Cameras on i.MX95, Part 1: From Photons to /dev/video

entry.content:
TL;DR: A camera on an embedded board is two links, not one: I²C to configure the sensor, and MIPI CSI-2 to stream pixels. On the i.MX95 the pixels go through a D-PHY receiver, a CSI-2 controller, a pixel formatter and the ISI, which writes frames to memory. If the sensor outputs RAW Bayer data, the NEO-ISP turns it into an image, and libcamera ties everything together. This post walks through each step, with interactive diagrams.

About this series

For a while now my day job has involved cameras on the NXP i.MX95: porting a third-party vendor kernel driver for an onsemi AR2020 image sensor, and writing the device tree that connects it to the SoC. Camera bring-up has a reputation for being hard, and part of the reason is that the knowledge is scattered across sensor datasheets, MIPI specifications, kernel documentation and vendor guides. This series is my attempt to put what I have learned in one place, in the order I wish I had learned it.

Part Topic
1 The big picture: from photons to /dev/video (this post)
2 The sensor driver: a V4L2 subdevice, power-up sequence, registers and controls
3 The device tree: describing the camera, endpoints, lanes and link frequency
4 Bring-up and debugging with media-ctl, v4l2-ctl and the media graph
5 libcamera and the NEO-ISP: from RAW to a good-looking image

This first part has no driver code. It builds the mental model the rest of the series hangs on: what each piece of hardware does, and why the Linux side is shaped the way it is.

Two links, not one

The first thing to understand about a MIPI camera is that it talks to the SoC over two separate interfaces:

  • I²C, for control. The sensor is an I²C device with hundreds of registers. Through them, the driver sets the resolution, frame rate, exposure time and analog gain, and starts or stops streaming. I²C is slow (hundreds of kHz), which is fine because it only carries a few bytes per frame.
  • MIPI CSI-2, for data. The pixels themselves flow over high-speed differential lanes at gigabits per second, in one direction only, from sensor to SoC.

Around those two links there are a few more signals that a driver has to get right: power supplies (typically separate analog, digital and I/O rails), an input clock for the sensor (often called MCLK or EXTCLK), and reset or power-down GPIOs. Most “the camera doesn’t probe” problems are one of these, long before any pixel moves.

Debugging rule of thumb. If the driver can’t read the sensor’s chip ID over I²C, the problem is power, clock, reset or the I²C address, not CSI-2. NXP’s porting guide lists the same order: supplies, MCLK, reset and power sequence.

The AR2020 at a glance

The sensor in this series is the onsemi AR2020, part of onsemi’s Hyperlux LP family:

Property Value
Resolution 20 MP, 5120 × 3840 active pixels
Optical size 1/1.8 inch
Pixel 1.4 µm, back-side illuminated (BSI)
Shutter Rolling shutter
Color RGB Bayer color filter
Output MIPI D-PHY, up to 2 × 4 lanes
Max speed Full resolution at up to 60 fps in 10-bit linear mode
Extras Binning/skipping, motion wake-up, enhanced near-infrared response

Two of these lines matter a lot for the rest of the series. “Bayer” means the sensor’s raw output is not a color image yet. And “up to 60 fps at full resolution” doesn’t mean the SoC can take it: we’ll check that with real numbers at the end of this post.

From photons to RAW: the Bayer mosaic

Each pixel of an image sensor is a photodiode that counts light. It has no idea what color the light was. To get color, the sensor puts a tiny color filter on top of every pixel, in a repeating 2 × 2 pattern: one red, two green, one blue. This is the Bayer pattern (RGGB, or a shifted variant such as GRBG), and green appears twice because human vision is most sensitive to it.

So the sensor sends one number per pixel: the brightness behind that pixel’s filter. In 10-bit mode that number is between 0 and 1023. This is what “RAW” or “RAW10” means. Turning that mosaic into a full-color image, by estimating the two missing colors at every pixel, is called demosaicing, and it is one of the main jobs of an ISP.

This interactive figure needs JavaScript.

MIPI CSI-2 on the wire

MIPI CSI-2 is really two layers:

  • D-PHY, the physical layer. One clock lane plus one to four data lanes, each a differential pair. Lanes have two modes: a low-power mode used between lines and frames, and a high-speed mode for bursts of pixel data. Clocking is double data rate, so a lane running at 1.77 Gbps uses a clock of about 885 MHz. That number, the link frequency, will come back in the driver and the device tree.
  • CSI-2, the protocol layer. The image is sent line by line in packets. Short packets mark frame start, frame end and, optionally, line start and line end. Each line of pixels travels in one long packet: a 4-byte header, the payload, and a 2-byte CRC.

The header’s first byte, the data identifier, combines a virtual channel (which stream this belongs to, so several streams can share one link) and a data type (for example 0x2B for RAW10, 0x1E for YUV422 8-bit). The receiver uses these to decide what to do with the packet. RAW10 is also packed: four 10-bit pixels travel as five bytes, the first four holding the 8 most significant bits of each pixel, the fifth holding the remaining 2-bit pieces.

With several lanes, the transmitter stripes the packet bytes across them, round robin, and the receiver merges them back in order. More lanes means the same packet takes less time on the wire:

This interactive figure needs JavaScript.

Inside the i.MX95 camera domain

NXP calls the camera part of the i.MX95 the camera domain. It has two camera interfaces: one with its own D-PHY, and one whose D-PHY is shared with a display (DSI) output. Each has a CSI-2 controller and a pixel formatter, followed by the ISI (Image Sensing Interface) and the NEO-ISP.

Step through the pipeline below. The toggle at the top switches between the two kinds of camera you can connect.

This interactive figure needs JavaScript.

The toggle exists because there are two very different kinds of MIPI camera:

  • A RAW sensor such as a bare AR2020 sends Bayer data. Something has to turn it into an image, and on the i.MX95 that is the NEO-ISP. The current NXP libcamera stack uses the ISP in memory-to-memory mode: the ISI first writes the RAW frame to DDR, then the ISP reads it back, processes it, and writes the final frame.
  • A “smart” camera module has its own ISP chip next to the sensor and sends ready-made YUV. In that case the i.MX95 only needs the CSI-2 receiver and the ISI. Some vendors sell AR2020 modules like this: TechNexion’s TEVS-AR2020, for example, integrates an ISP and can output both YUV and RAW.

Which kind you have changes almost everything above the sensor driver: which libcamera pipeline handler is used, whether you need ISP tuning files, and how you debug image quality. It is the first question to answer in any camera project.

The software side: V4L2, the media controller and libcamera

Every hardware block above has its own Linux driver, and all of them use the kernel’s V4L2 (Video4Linux2) framework. Older V4L2 hardware was simple enough to hide behind a single /dev/video0. Modern SoC camera pipelines are not, so V4L2 splits them up:

  • Each block (sensor, CSI-2 receiver, formatter, ISI, ISP) is a V4L2 subdevice, with its own /dev/v4l-subdevN node and pads where data comes in and goes out.
  • The media controller API, through /dev/mediaN, exposes the whole graph: which entity is linked to which, and with what format on each pad.
  • Only the blocks that touch memory, the ISI outputs and the ISP inputs and outputs, are video devices with /dev/videoN nodes.

Configuring all of that by hand is painful, which is why NXP’s stack uses libcamera on top. It has two parts that matter here:

  • A pipeline handler knows the platform’s media graph and configures it. NXP provides one for the ISI-only path and one for the NEO-ISP path.
  • An IPA (image processing algorithm) module runs the “3A” algorithms: auto exposure, auto white balance and, on some cameras, auto focus. It reads statistics from the ISP and writes new exposure and gain values back to the sensor driver, which sends them over I²C.

That last point is why a sensor driver for the NEO-ISP path has to expose a specific set of V4L2 controls. NXP’s porting guide lists them: link frequency, pixel rate, horizontal and vertical blanking, exposure, analog gain, orientation and rotation. Without them libcamera can’t calculate frame timing or run auto exposure. We’ll implement these in Part 2.

Will it fit? A bandwidth check

Before writing any code, check that the SoC can actually receive the camera mode you want. NXP’s guide gives the method:

  1. Link bandwidth = width × height × bits per pixel × fps × (1 + blanking). NXP suggests assuming 20% blanking overhead if you don’t have exact timings. Each i.MX95 camera interface can carry up to 10 Gbps, which is 2.5 Gbps per lane with four lanes.
  2. Pixel clock = width × height × fps × (1 + blanking), divided by the pixels moved per clock cycle. The formatter, ISI and ISP all run from the cam_isi_clk_root clock: 333.33 MHz in low drive mode, 500 MHz nominal, 666.67 MHz in override mode. RAW32 mode moves 2 pixels per clock for RAW10/12 and 4 for RAW8. YUV and RGB always move 1 pixel per clock.

Try it with the AR2020’s modes:

This interactive figure needs JavaScript.

The full-resolution 30 fps RAW10 mode works out like this:

Quantity Calculation Result
Link bandwidth 5120 × 3840 × 10 × 30 × 1.2 7.08 Gbps (≤ 10)
Per lane, 4 lanes 7.08 / 4 1.77 Gbps (≤ 2.5)
Link frequency 1.77 / 2 ≈ 885 MHz
Pixel clock, RAW32 on (2 px/clk) 5120 × 3840 × 30 × 1.2 / 2 354 MHz (≤ 500)
Pixel clock, RAW32 off 5120 × 3840 × 30 × 1.2 708 MHz (> 666.67)

Two lessons hide in that table. First, the 30 fps mode only fits with RAW32 mode enabled: without it, the camera domain clock can’t keep up even in override mode. Second, the sensor’s maximum of 60 fps at full resolution needs about 14 Gbps, more than one i.MX95 camera interface can carry, so that mode isn’t usable here regardless of software. On the “smart module” path the picture changes again: YUV422 uses 16 bits per pixel and always moves one pixel per clock, so full-resolution YUV needs a much lower frame rate.

Key terms

Term Meaning
Bayer / RAW Sensor output with one color sample per pixel, before demosaicing
D-PHY MIPI physical layer: clock lane + data lanes, low-power and high-speed modes
CSI-2 MIPI camera protocol: packets with data type and virtual channel
Link frequency D-PHY clock, half the per-lane bit rate
ISI i.MX Image Sensing Interface: writes frames to memory, converts, scales
NEO-ISP i.MX95 image signal processor: RAW to image, plus statistics for 3A
V4L2 subdevice A kernel driver for one block in the pipeline, with input and output pads
Media controller Kernel API describing the pipeline as a graph of linked entities
Pipeline handler libcamera component that configures one platform’s media graph
IPA / 3A Auto exposure, auto white balance and auto focus algorithms

What’s next

Now that the path from sensor to memory is clear, Part 2 goes to the first box in the diagram: the sensor driver. We’ll look at what a V4L2 subdevice driver for the AR2020 has to do, from the power-up sequence to the controls libcamera relies on, and at what changes when you port a driver written by a third-party vendor for another platform.

References

  • NXP UG10215: i.MX 95x Camera Porting Guide (Rev. 2.5, September 2026)
  • onsemi AR2020 product page and datasheet
  • TechNexion TEVS-AR2020 camera module
  • Linux kernel: Video4Linux (V4L2) driver API
  • Linux kernel: Pixel data transmitter and receiver drivers (CSI-2)
  • libcamera documentation
  • RidgeRun: NXP i.MX95 capture subsystem
entry.summary: The first post in a series on embedded cameras on the NXP i.MX95. How a MIPI CSI-2 camera like the onsemi AR2020 gets an image into memory, block by block, with interactive diagrams.

entry.title: Linux and FreeRTOS on One Chip: RPmsg on the i.MX8M Mini

link.title: Linux and FreeRTOS on One Chip: RPmsg on the i.MX8M Mini

entry.content:
TL;DR: The i.MX8M Mini has Cortex-A53 cores for Linux and a Cortex-M4 for real-time work. I built a Toradex Yocto image, started a FreeRTOS firmware on the M4 from U-Boot, added a device tree that reserves shared memory and describes the M4 to Linux, and exchanged messages between the two cores through /dev/ttyRPMSG30.

Device tree and original notes: github.com/parsamajidi21/RPmsg-Device-Tree

Introduction

Many modern SoCs pair “big” application cores with a small microcontroller core. The NXP i.MX8M Mini is a good example: up to four Cortex-A53 cores that run Linux, and one Cortex-M4F that can run bare metal or an RTOS. Running different operating systems on different cores of the same chip is called asymmetric multiprocessing (AMP).

The appeal is simple. Linux is great at networking, storage and user interfaces, but it is not a hard real-time OS. The M4 can handle the time-critical part (motor control, sensor sampling, a safety watchdog) with predictable latency, while Linux does everything else. For that to work, the two sides need a way to talk. On NXP parts that way is RPmsg, a message bus built on virtio and shared memory.

In this post I walk through the setup I built on a Toradex Verdin i.MX8M Mini: building the Linux image, starting firmware on the M4, writing the device tree that glues the two together, and finally sending messages from Linux to FreeRTOS. Along the way I explain what each address and device tree node is for, because that is the part most guides skip.

Setup

Item Version / model
SoM Toradex Verdin i.MX8M Mini Quad 2GB WB IT V1.1A (product ID 0055)
Carrier Toradex Dahlia V1.0C
BSP Toradex BSP 6.3.0
Yocto 4.0 (Kirkstone)
Kernel Toradex downstream 5.15.77, based on NXP BSP L5.15_2.1.0
M4 firmware FreeRTOS demos from the NXP MCUXpresso SDK for evkmimx8mm
M4 toolchain GNU Arm Embedded (arm-none-eabi-gcc)

How the pieces fit together

Before the commands, here is the whole flow. Everything later in the post is one of these steps.

  1. U-Boot copies the M4 firmware into the M4’s tightly coupled memory (TCM) and releases the M4 from reset (bootaux).
  2. The FreeRTOS firmware starts, publishes a resource table in shared DDR describing the communication buffers it expects, and waits.
  3. Linux boots on the A53 cores. The device tree tells it which DDR regions are shared with the M4, so Linux keeps its hands off them.
  4. The imx_rproc remoteproc driver sees that the M4 is already running, attaches to it, reads the resource table and creates a virtio device for the RPmsg bus.
  5. The two cores exchange messages through two ring buffers (vrings) in shared memory, and poke each other with interrupts through the Messaging Unit (MU).
  6. The M4 announces a named channel, rpmsg-virtual-tty-channel-1. The imx_rpmsg_tty driver binds to it and creates /dev/ttyRPMSG30. Writing to that file sends a message to the M4.

Step 1: Build the Linux image with Yocto

Toradex ships its BSP as a repo manifest. First install the repo tool:

mkdir -p ~/bin
export PATH=~/bin:$PATH
curl https://commondatastorage.googleapis.com/git-repo-downloads/repo > ~/bin/repo
chmod a+x ~/bin/repo

Then fetch the Kirkstone-based BSP and set up the build environment:

mkdir -p ~/oe-core && cd ~/oe-core
repo init -u git://git.toradex.com/toradex-manifest.git -b kirkstone-6.x.y -m tdxref/default.xml
repo sync
. export   # sets up the shell and creates build/conf/*.conf on first run

Sourcing export only affects the current shell, so repeat it in every new terminal.

In build/conf/local.conf, select the machine and accept the NXP EULA (needed for some NXP firmware and libraries pulled in by meta-freescale):

MACHINE ?= "verdin-imx8mm"
ACCEPT_FSL_EULA = "1"

I built the minimal command-line reference image:

bitbake tdx-reference-minimal-image

The first build takes a few hours. The output, including the Toradex Easy Installer tarball, lands in build/deploy/images/verdin-imx8mm/.

Step 2: Flash the image

Toradex modules are flashed with the Toradex Easy Installer (Tezi). If the module isn’t already running it:

  1. Download the Tezi archive for the Verdin iMX8M Mini and unpack it on the host.
  2. Put the module in recovery mode: open jumper JP3, then hold the Recovery button (SW5) while pressing ON/OFF (SW3), and keep holding Recovery for about 10 more seconds.

  3. On the host, run the loader from the unpacked archive:

    sudo ./recovery-linux.sh

Then extract the image tarball from deploy/images/ onto a FAT32 USB drive, plug it into the carrier board, and install it from the Tezi interface (I connected to it over VNC).

Step 3: First firmware on the Cortex-M4

Before adding RPmsg, it is worth checking that we can run anything at all on the M4.

Build hello_world

Download the MCUXpresso SDK for the EVK-MIMX8MM board (Toradex’s FreeRTOS guide explains which options to pick), and install a bare-metal Arm toolchain:

sudo apt-get install gcc-arm-none-eabi binutils-arm-none-eabi
export ARMGCC_DIR=/usr   # or the path of an extracted toolchain tarball

Build the demo:

cd <sdk>/boards/evkmimx8mm/demo_apps/hello_world/armgcc
./build_all.sh

build_all.sh builds debug and release variants for each memory target. The release, TCM build gives release/hello_world.bin. Copy it to a FAT32 SD card and insert the card in the carrier board’s SD slot.

Two serial consoles

The Dahlia carrier has a USB-to-serial chip on its debug USB-C port (X18) that exposes four ports on the host. On my setup, /dev/ttyUSB3 was the Linux/U-Boot console (UART3), and /dev/ttyUSB2 was the M4 debug UART (UART4). I used tmux to keep one picocom session for each in the same window:

sudo picocom -b 115200 /dev/ttyUSB3   # top pane: U-Boot / Linux
sudo picocom -b 115200 /dev/ttyUSB2   # bottom pane: Cortex-M4

Power on the board and press a key to stop autoboot. You land in the U-Boot shell:

Start the M4 from U-Boot

Verdin iMX8MM # setenv m4addr 0x7e0000
Verdin iMX8MM # saveenv
Verdin iMX8MM # fatload mmc 1 0x48000000 hello_world.bin && dcache flush && cp.b 0x48000000 ${m4addr} 0x20000
Verdin iMX8MM # bootaux ${m4addr}

Each command has a reason:

  • m4addr = 0x7e0000 is where the A53 cores see the M4’s TCML, the 128 KB tightly coupled code memory. The M4 sees the same memory at 0x1FFE0000. saveenv keeps the variable across reboots.
  • fatload mmc 1 0x48000000 hello_world.bin reads the file from the SD card (mmc 1 is the SD controller, FSL_SDHC: 1 in the boot log) into a scratch area of DDR at 0x48000000.
  • dcache flush writes the A53 data cache back to memory, so the bytes really are in RAM and not only in the A53’s cache.
  • cp.b 0x48000000 ${m4addr} 0x20000 copies 128 KB (the full TCML size) from DDR into the TCM.
  • bootaux ${m4addr} releases the M4 from reset.

The bootaux output is a nice sanity check. An Arm Cortex-M image starts with its vector table: the first word is the initial stack pointer, the second is the reset handler. U-Boot reads both from the image and prints them:

## Starting auxiliary core stack = 0x20020000, pc = 0x1FFE030D...

0x1FFE030D is inside the TCML as the M4 sees it (the odd last bit just marks Thumb code), and 0x20020000 is the top of the 128 KB data TCM (TCMU, which starts at 0x20000000). If those numbers look wrong, you copied the wrong file or the wrong build target.

Step 4: A device tree for RPmsg

Running the M4 next to Linux is not enough. Linux also has to know:

  • which memory belongs to the M4 or is shared with it, so it never allocates those pages for itself;
  • that there is a remote core and how to talk to it (mailbox, resource table, vrings);
  • which peripherals the M4 owns, so Linux doesn’t reconfigure or power them down.

The stock Verdin device trees don’t describe any of this. NXP’s EVK has an RPmsg variant, imx8mm-evk-rpmsg.dts, so I took its RPmsg parts and combined them with the Verdin includes. The full file is imx8mm-verdin-wifi-dev-rpmsg.dts. The interesting parts follow.

Base board

#include "imx8mm-verdin.dtsi"
#include "imx8mm-verdin-wifi.dtsi"
#include "imx8mm-verdin-dev.dtsi"

These pull in the SoM, the Wi-Fi/Bluetooth variant, and the carrier description, the same as Toradex’s own imx8mm-verdin-wifi-dev.dts.

Reserved memory

reserved-memory {
    #address-cells = <2>;
    #size-cells = <2>;
    ranges;

    m4_reserved: m4@0x80000000 {
        no-map;
        reg = <0 0x80000000 0 0x1000000>;
    };

    vdev0vring0: vdev0vring0@b8000000 {
        reg = <0 0xb8000000 0 0x8000>;
        no-map;
    };

    vdev0vring1: vdev0vring1@b8008000 {
        reg = <0 0xb8008000 0 0x8000>;
        no-map;
    };

    rsc_table: rsc_table@b80ff000 {
        reg = <0 0xb80ff000 0 0x1000>;
        no-map;
    };

    vdevbuffer: vdevbuffer@b8400000 {
        compatible = "shared-dma-pool";
        reg = <0 0xb8400000 0 0x100000>;
        no-map;
    };
};
Region Address Size Purpose
m4_reserved 0x80000000 16 MB DDR for M4 code and data, if the firmware is built to run from DDR
vdev0vring0 0xb8000000 32 KB First virtio ring (one direction)
vdev0vring1 0xb8008000 32 KB Second virtio ring (the other direction)
rsc_table 0xb80ff000 4 KB Resource table written by the M4 firmware
vdevbuffer 0xb8400000 1 MB Pool for the message buffers themselves

no-map removes the region from Linux’s memory map entirely, so nothing in Linux can use it by accident. These addresses are not arbitrary: they must match what the FreeRTOS firmware was built with. The SDK demos for evkmimx8mm use exactly these values, which is why reusing the EVK layout works.

The remote core

imx8mm-cm4 {
    compatible = "fsl,imx8mm-cm4";
    rsc-da = <0xb8000000>;
    clocks = <&clk IMX8MM_CLK_M4_DIV>;
    mbox-names = "tx", "rx", "rxdb";
    mboxes = <&mu 0 1
          &mu 1 1
          &mu 3 1>;
    memory-region = <&vdevbuffer>, <&vdev0vring0>, <&vdev0vring1>, <&rsc_table>;
    syscon = <&src>;
    fsl,startup-delay-ms = <500>;
};

This node binds the imx_rproc remoteproc driver (drivers/remoteproc/imx_rproc.c). The properties that matter:

  • memory-region hands the vrings, the buffer pool and the resource table to the driver.
  • mboxes uses three channels of the Messaging Unit, a hardware block that lets one core raise an interrupt on the other: transmit, receive, and a receive doorbell. The data travels through shared memory; the MU only says “there is something new”.
  • syscon = <&src> gives the driver access to the System Reset Controller. In the NXP 5.15 kernel, imx_rproc reads the M4 reset bits there at probe time. If the M4 is not held in reset, the driver concludes that someone (U-Boot, in our case) already started it, and attaches instead of loading firmware itself.

Two properties are inherited from the EVK file but don’t do anything in this setup, as far as I can tell from the NXP lf-5.15 source: rsc-da isn’t read by imx_rproc at all, and fsl,startup-delay-ms is only applied when Linux starts the core itself, not when it attaches.

Peripherals owned by the M4

&uart4 {
    status = "disabled";
};

UART4 is the M4’s debug console. If Linux enabled it too, both cores would fight over the same UART. The file also has an init-on-array on the clock controller (an NXP downstream property). It lists clocks such as IMX8MM_CLK_UART4_ROOT that Linux must keep running even though no Linux driver uses them, so the M4’s peripherals don’t stop when Linux turns off unused clocks.

The rest of the file (rpmsg_audio, and disabling sai1, sai3, sdma3 and the WM8524 codec) comes from the EVK’s RPmsg audio setup, where the M4 plays audio while Linux sleeps. It isn’t needed for the TTY demo. You can even see it in the kernel log later: imx-audio-rpmsg: no reserved DMA memory. A cleaner version of this file would drop those nodes.

Adding it to the build

I placed the file next to the other i.MX device trees in the kernel source and added it to the device tree Makefile:

dtb-$(CONFIG_ARCH_MXC) += imx8mm-verdin-wifi-dev-rpmsg.dtb

Then I added it to KERNEL_DEVICETREE in the machine configuration (layers/meta-toradex-nxp/conf/machine/verdin-imx8mm.conf), so the build actually produces it and installs it into the image:

KERNEL_DEVICETREE = " \
    freescale/imx8mm-verdin-nonwifi-dahlia.dtb \
    freescale/imx8mm-verdin-nonwifi-dev.dtb \
    freescale/imx8mm-verdin-nonwifi-yavia.dtb \
    freescale/imx8mm-verdin-wifi-dahlia.dtb \
    freescale/imx8mm-verdin-wifi-dev.dtb \
    freescale/imx8mm-verdin-wifi-yavia.dtb \
    freescale/imx8mm-verdin-wifi-dev-rpmsg.dtb \
"

Finally I pointed TORADEX_PRODUCT_IDS for my module (product ID 0055, printed in the U-Boot banner) at the new device tree. The Toradex image classes use this mapping to generate the Easy Installer metadata, which says which device tree goes with which module:

TORADEX_PRODUCT_IDS[0055] = "imx8mm-verdin-wifi-v1.1-dev-rpmsg.dtb"

Rebuild the image with bitbake and flash it again as in step 2.

A cleaner way. Editing files in tmp/work-shared/.../kernel-source and in Toradex’s own layer works for a quick experiment, but bitbake -c cleanall throws away changes in work-shared, and the next repo sync can conflict with or overwrite edits in a vendor layer. For anything you want to keep, put them in your own layer: the .dts as a kernel patch in a linux-toradex_%.bbappend (SRC_URI:append = " file://0001-arm64-dts-add-verdin-rpmsg.patch"), and KERNEL_DEVICETREE:append = " freescale/imx8mm-verdin-wifi-dev-rpmsg.dtb" in your layer’s config or local.conf.

Step 5: Talk to the M4 over RPmsg

Build the RPmsg firmware

The SDK has two FreeRTOS RPmsg demos in boards/evkmimx8mm/multicore_examples/: rpmsg_lite_pingpong_rtos and rpmsg_lite_str_echo_rtos. I used the string echo demo, which prints every message it receives:

cd <sdk>/boards/evkmimx8mm/multicore_examples/rpmsg_lite_str_echo_rtos/armgcc
./build_all.sh

Copy rpmsg_lite_str_echo_rtos.bin to the SD card.

Start it from U-Boot

Same commands as before, just a different file (m4addr is already saved):

Verdin iMX8MM # fatload mmc 1 0x48000000 rpmsg_lite_str_echo_rtos.bin && dcache flush && cp.b 0x48000000 ${m4addr} 0x20000
Verdin iMX8MM # bootaux ${m4addr}

Then type boot in the U-Boot console to start Linux. The order matters: the M4 must be running before Linux boots, otherwise imx_rproc finds it in reset and there is nothing to attach to.

Send messages from Linux

Once Linux is up, load the RPmsg TTY driver and write to the new device:

modprobe imx_rpmsg_tty
echo "hello world!" > /dev/ttyRPMSG30

The kernel log shows what happened on the Linux side:

imx_rpmsg_tty virtio0.rpmsg-virtual-tty-channel-1.-1.30: new channel: 0x400 -> 0x1e!
Install rpmsg tty driver!
  • virtio0 is the virtio device that imx_rproc created after attaching to the M4.
  • rpmsg-virtual-tty-channel-1 is the channel name the M4 announced (“Nameservice sent” on the M4 console). imx_rpmsg_tty matches on that name.
  • 0x400 -> 0x1e are the endpoint addresses: Linux’s local endpoint 0x400 talks to the M4’s endpoint 0x1e, which is 30 in decimal. The driver names the device after the remote endpoint, which is where ttyRPMSG30 comes from.

On the M4 console every message arrives with its length:

Get Message From Master Side : "hello world!" [len : 12]

Troubleshooting notes

  • Wrong stack/pc from bootaux: the image isn’t a TCM build, or the copy failed. Check the file size with ls mmc 1 and the build target in build_all.sh’s output.
  • No /dev/ttyRPMSG30: check that Linux booted with the RPmsg device tree (cat /proc/device-tree/model), that the M4 was started before boot, and that the M4 console printed “Nameservice sent”.
  • Kernel crashes or random memory corruption: a reserved region is missing or doesn’t match the firmware’s memory layout. The addresses in the device tree and in the firmware must agree.
  • The M4 stops printing after Linux boots: Linux probably disabled a clock or claimed a peripheral the M4 uses. Check init-on-array and the status = "disabled" nodes.

Conclusion

The demo itself is just text going from one core to another, but getting there touches most layers of an embedded Linux system: a Yocto BSP, the bootloader, a hand-written device tree, a remoteproc driver and a bare-metal toolchain. The main lesson for me was that the device tree is the contract between the two worlds. The memory map, the mailbox and the peripheral ownership all have to agree with the firmware on the other core, and the kernel trusts whatever you write there.

A natural next step is to let Linux start the M4 itself: imx_rproc can also load the firmware ELF from /lib/firmware through the remoteproc sysfs interface, which removes the manual U-Boot step.

References

  • Original notes and device tree (GitHub)
  • Toradex: Build a Reference Image with Yocto Project/OpenEmbedded
  • Toradex: FreeRTOS on the Cortex-M4 of a Verdin iMX8M Mini
  • Toradex: Device Tree Overview
  • NXP linux-imx imx_rproc.c (lf-5.15.y)
  • Kynetics: Asymmetric Multiprocessing, RPMsg device and driver on Linux and Android
  • Kynetics: An Introduction to Asymmetric Multiprocessing (ELC 2018)
  • Asymmetric Multiprocessing and Embedded Linux (eLinux)
entry.summary: Running FreeRTOS on the Cortex-M4 next to Linux on the Cortex-A53 cores of a Toradex Verdin i.MX8M Mini, and making them talk over RPmsg. Yocto build, U-Boot bootaux, a custom device tree, and what each piece actually does.

entry.title: Dynamic Layers in Yocto
entry.content:
Introduction

Hi, this is my first official blog post since my graduation. I’ve been working with Dynamic Layers in Yocto for a while, and I thought it would be a good idea to share what I’ve learned, since I remember there weren’t many resources available on this topic when I was learning.

Throughout the post I use meta-raspberrypi as the main reference, because it is one of the cleanest real-world examples of the pattern. All its snippets are taken from the master branch (commit 863444d, October 2026).

Then I’ll show where I actually ran into dynamic layers: Ezurio’s meta-summit-som, where I worked on the kernel recipes for the NXP i.MX95 platform.

The problem: optional integrations

Imagine you maintain a BSP layer for a board. The board has a camera, a GPU, and a few HATs, and you want good integration with the wider ecosystem:

  • If the user builds with meta-multimedia, libcamera should be built with your board’s camera pipeline enabled.
  • If they use meta-qt5, qtbase should be configured for your GPU.
  • If they use meta-python, a Python library for your sensor board should be available.

None of these layers is required to boot the board, so you don’t want to force them on every user. But a normal .bbappend has a sharp edge: if the recipe it appends to doesn’t exist, BitBake stops with an error.

ERROR: No recipes in default available for:
  /path/to/meta-mybsp/recipes-qt/qt5/qtbase_%.bbappend

Older releases let you downgrade this to a warning with BB_DANGLINGAPPENDS_WARNONLY, which also hid real mistakes. Current BitBake has dropped that escape hatch: a bbappend without a recipe is always fatal. So without dynamic layers you’re left with two bad options:

  1. Add every optional layer to LAYERDEPENDS and force users to download layers they don’t need.
  2. Split the integration into many small layers (meta-mybsp-qt5, meta-mybsp-multimedia, …) that users have to discover and add themselves.

Dynamic layers are the clean third option.

What are Dynamic Layers?

A dynamic layer is a sub-directory of your layer whose recipes and bbappends are only parsed when a specific other layer is part of the build. The mechanism is a single variable in conf/layer.conf: BBFILES_DYNAMIC.

Each entry has the form:

<collection-name>:<file-glob>
  • <collection-name> is the name another layer registers in its own layer.conf via BBFILE_COLLECTIONS. It is not the directory name of the layer. For example, meta-oe registers itself as openembedded-layer.
  • <file-glob> is the set of .bb / .bbappend files to add to BBFILES, but only if that collection is present.

If the collection isn’t in the build, the files are simply never parsed. No dangling-append errors, and no extra dependencies.

The BitBake manual also documents the inverse: prefixing the collection with ! (e.g. !clang-layer:...) includes the files only when that layer is absent, which is handy for backfilling a recipe the other layer would otherwise provide.

How meta-raspberrypi uses them

The layer.conf

Here is the relevant part of meta-raspberrypi/conf/layer.conf:

BBFILE_COLLECTIONS += "raspberrypi"
BBFILE_PATTERN_raspberrypi := "^${LAYERDIR}/"
BBFILE_PRIORITY_raspberrypi = "9"

LAYERDEPENDS_raspberrypi = "core"

# The dynamic-layers directory hosts the extensions and layer specific
# modifications.
#
# The .bbappend and .bb files are included if the respective layer
# collection is available.
BBFILES_DYNAMIC += " \
    openembedded-layer:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/openembedded-layer/*/*/*.bb \
    openembedded-layer:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/openembedded-layer/*/*/*.bbappend \
    networking-layer:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/networking-layer/*/*/*.bb \
    networking-layer:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/networking-layer/*/*/*.bbappend \
    qt5-layer:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/qt5-layer/*/*/*.bb \
    qt5-layer:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/qt5-layer/*/*/*.bbappend \
    multimedia-layer:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/multimedia-layer/*/*/*.bb \
    multimedia-layer:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/multimedia-layer/*/*/*.bbappend \
    meta-python:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/meta-python/*/*/*.bb \
    meta-python:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/meta-python/*/*/*.bbappend \
"

Two things stand out:

  • The only hard dependency is core. Everything else is optional.
  • Each sub-directory is named after the collection it depends on. This isn’t required by BitBake, but it’s a convention worth copying: you can tell from the path which layer activates a file.

The directory layout

The globs */*/*.bb mean “recipe category / recipe name / file”, the same structure as a normal layer:

meta-raspberrypi/dynamic-layers/
├── meta-python/          # active only with meta-python
│   ├── recipes-connectivity/lirc/
│   ├── recipes-core/packagegroups/
│   └── recipes-devtools/python/
├── multimedia-layer/     # active only with meta-multimedia
│   └── recipes-multimedia/
│       ├── libcamera/
│       ├── libcamera-apps/
│       ├── libpisp/
│       └── rpidistro-vlc/
├── networking-layer/     # active only with meta-networking
│   └── recipes-support/drbd/
├── openembedded-layer/   # active only with meta-oe
│   ├── recipes-core/packagegroups/
│   └── recipes-devtools/python/
└── qt5-layer/            # active only with meta-qt5
    └── recipes-qt/qt5/
Directory Activated by collection Provided by layer
openembedded-layer openembedded-layer meta-oe
networking-layer networking-layer meta-networking
multimedia-layer multimedia-layer meta-multimedia
meta-python meta-python meta-python
qt5-layer qt5-layer meta-qt5

What goes inside: four patterns

Looking through the dynamic-layers tree, the files fall into a few distinct patterns.

1. Tuning another layer’s recipe for your hardware

multimedia-layer/recipes-multimedia/libcamera/libcamera_%.bbappend:

EXTRA_OEMESON:append:rpi = " -Dipas=rpi/vc4,rpi/pisp"
PACKAGECONFIG:append:rpi = " raspberrypi"
CXXFLAGS:append:rpi = " -Wno-unaligned-access "

libcamera comes from meta-multimedia. The bbappend enables the Raspberry Pi image processing algorithms (VC4 and PiSP). Without meta-multimedia there is no libcamera to append to, so the file must not be parsed. That’s exactly what the dynamic layer guarantees.

Note the :rpi override: even when the dynamic layer is active, the changes only apply when building for a Raspberry Pi machine. Activation by layer and activation by machine are two separate filters, and good BSPs use both.

The qt5-layer/recipes-qt/qt5/qtbase_%.bbappend follows the same idea on a bigger scale. It selects eglfs/gles2/kms depending on DISTRO_FEATURES and MACHINE_FEATURES, and adds the right EGLFS device integration for the Pi GPU.

2. Shipping new recipes that need another layer

multimedia-layer/recipes-multimedia/libcamera-apps/libcamera-apps_1.9.0.bb is a full recipe, not an append:

PROVIDES += "rpicam-apps"

DEPENDS = "libcamera libexif jpeg tiff libpng boost"

It DEPENDS on libcamera, which only exists in meta-multimedia. If this recipe lived in the main layer, anyone building without meta-multimedia would get a “Nothing PROVIDES ‘libcamera’” error as soon as something pulled it in. Placing it under dynamic-layers/multimedia-layer/ ties its existence to its dependency.

The same goes for libpisp, the Pi-specific rpidistro-vlc build, and the Adafruit CircuitPython recipes under openembedded-layer/.

3. Opting out of something that doesn’t work on your board

networking-layer/recipes-support/drbd/drbd_%.bbappend:

COMPATIBLE_MACHINE:rpi = "(null)"

Dynamic layers aren’t only for adding things. Here meta-raspberrypi marks the drbd recipe from meta-networking as incompatible with Raspberry Pi machines. openembedded-layer/recipes-core/packagegroups/packagegroup-meta-oe.bbappend does something similar:

RDEPENDS:packagegroup-meta-oe-kernel:remove:rpi = "bpftool"

This drops bpftool from meta-oe’s kernel packagegroup, but only for Pi machines.

4. Extending your own recipes when an optional layer is available

meta-python/recipes-core/packagegroups/packagegroup-rpi-test.bbappend:

RDEPENDS:${PN} += "python3-sense-hat"

This one is subtle. packagegroup-rpi-test lives in meta-raspberrypi’s own main layer. The append adds python3-sense-hat, a recipe the dynamic layer itself provides, which in turn needs meta-python. So the test packagegroup automatically grows extra content when meta-python is there, and stays buildable when it isn’t.

Real-world example: meta-summit-som on i.MX95

My own hands-on experience with dynamic layers comes from Ezurio’s meta-summit-som (branch wrynose-summit-7.2.0.x), where I worked on the kernel recipes for the i.MX95 platform. meta-raspberrypi shows the textbook version of the pattern; this layer shows what it looks like in a production BSP, and it uses dynamic layers in a way meta-raspberrypi doesn’t.

One layer, several vendor BSPs

Here is the BBFILES_DYNAMIC block from its conf/layer.conf:

BBFILES_DYNAMIC += " \
    fsl-bsp-release:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/imx-bsp/recipes-*/*/*.bb \
    fsl-bsp-release:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/imx-bsp/recipes-*/*/*.bbappend \
    meta-ti-bsp:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/ti-bsp/recipes-*/*/*.bb \
    meta-ti-bsp:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/ti-bsp/recipes-*/*/*.bbappend \
    summit-radio:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/summit-radio/recipes-*/*/*.bb \
    summit-radio:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/summit-radio/recipes-*/*/*.bbappend \
    meta-aws:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/aws/recipes-*/*/*.bb \
    meta-aws:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/aws/recipes-*/*/*.bbappend \
    "

In meta-raspberrypi, dynamic layers add optional extras to a single-SoC BSP. Here they do something bigger: the same layer supports SoMs built on both NXP i.MX and TI SoCs, and the dynamic layers pick the right half:

  • Build with NXP’s BSP (meta-imx, whose meta-imx-bsp layer registers the fsl-bsp-release collection) and everything under dynamic-layers/imx-bsp/ comes alive: U-Boot, ATF, the i.MX95 System Manager and OEI, security tooling, and the kernel.
  • Build with TI’s BSP (meta-ti-bsp) and dynamic-layers/ti-bsp/ is used instead.
  • Neither vendor BSP is a hard dependency of the layer.

Two details differ from meta-raspberrypi:

  • The directory names don’t match the collection names. imx-bsp/ is activated by fsl-bsp-release, and aws/ by meta-aws. That’s perfectly legal, since BitBake only looks at the prefix before the colon. It’s just less self-documenting, so you need layer.conf open to know what activates what.
  • The globs are stricter: recipes-*/*/*.bb instead of */*/*.bb, so stray directories that don’t follow the recipes- naming are never parsed.

Inside the i.MX kernel recipe

Everything kernel-related for the i.MX family lives in one append, dynamic-layers/imx-bsp/recipes-kernel/linux-imx/linux-imx_%.bbappend, next to a directory of patches and per-SoC files:

recipes-kernel/linux-imx/
├── linux-imx_%.bbappend
└── linux-imx/
    ├── 0001-ts3a227-jack.patch
    ├── ...                         # ~50 kernel patches
    ├── mx8mm-generic-bsp/
    ├── mx8mp-generic-bsp/
    ├── mx91-generic-bsp/
    ├── mx93-generic-bsp/
    └── mx95-generic-bsp/
        ├── dts/freescale/          # i.MX95 device trees and overlays
        └── nitrogen_imx95_defconfig

The interesting part is how a single bbappend serves five SoCs. Here is a trimmed version:

FILESEXTRAPATHS:prepend := "${THISDIR}/${PN}:"

SRC_URI:append:summitsom = " \
    file://0001-ts3a227-jack.patch \
    ...
    file://dts \
    ${KERNEL_CONFIG_SUMMIT} \
    "

KERNEL_CONFIG_SUMMIT:mx8mm-generic-bsp = "file://nitrogen_imx8mm_defconfig"
KERNEL_CONFIG_SUMMIT:mx8mp-generic-bsp = "file://nitrogen_imx8mp_defconfig"
KERNEL_CONFIG_SUMMIT:mx91-generic-bsp = "file://nitrogen_imx91_defconfig"
KERNEL_CONFIG_SUMMIT:mx93-generic-bsp = "file://nitrogen_imx93_defconfig"
KERNEL_CONFIG_SUMMIT:mx95-generic-bsp = "file://nitrogen_imx95_defconfig"

do_patch:append:summitsom () {
    cp -af -t "${S}/arch/arm64/boot" "${UNPACKDIR}/dts"
}

Three mechanisms stack on top of each other here:

  1. Collection: the whole file only exists in the build when NXP’s BSP is present (the dynamic layer).
  2. Machine: every change is guarded by the :summitsom override, so other i.MX machines in the same build tree are untouched.
  3. SoC: mx95-generic-bsp is a machine override that meta-freescale adds for every i.MX95 machine. It does two jobs:
    • It selects the defconfig through KERNEL_CONFIG_SUMMIT:mx95-generic-bsp.
    • Because the fetcher searches override-named sub-directories first (via FILESOVERRIDES, which includes the machine overrides), the generic file://dts resolves to linux-imx/mx95-generic-bsp/dts on an i.MX95 build and to the matching directory for each other SoC. The do_patch append then copies those device trees into the kernel source tree.

On i.MX95 this matters a lot. mx95-generic-bsp/dts/freescale/ holds a base carrier-board device tree plus a long list of overlays (.dtso): MIPI-CSI cameras (OV5640, OV5645, Arducam Pivariety), MIPI-DSI and LVDS panels, and M.2 Wi-Fi/Bluetooth modules over SDIO, UART, and PCIe. Each SoC keeps its own device trees and kernel config in its own folder, while the shared patches and build logic stay in one append. Adding a new SoC is mostly a matter of adding a new mxNN-generic-bsp/ directory and one KERNEL_CONFIG_SUMMIT line.

What it taught me

  • Dynamic layers are how a multi-vendor BSP stays a single layer. Without them, the i.MX and TI halves would have to be separate layers, or the layer would have to depend on both vendors’ BSPs.
  • The dynamic layer is only the first filter. In practice I relied just as much on the machine override (:summitsom) and the SoC override (mx95-generic-bsp) to make sure a change hit exactly the boards I intended.
  • Know where a file comes from. Between FILESEXTRAPATHS, override sub-directories, and dynamic layers, the same file://dts can mean five different directories. When something doesn’t build, bitbake -e linux-imx | grep ^FILESPATH= and bitbake-layers show-appends answer “which file did BitBake actually pick?” faster than reading recipes.

Adding a dynamic layer to your own layer

Say you maintain meta-mybsp and want optional Qt and meta-oe integrations.

1. Create the directories, named after the collections:

meta-mybsp/
├── conf/layer.conf
├── recipes-bsp/...
└── dynamic-layers/
    ├── qt5-layer/
    │   └── recipes-qt/qt5/qtbase_%.bbappend
    └── openembedded-layer/
        └── recipes-support/my-tool/my-tool_1.0.bb

2. Register them in conf/layer.conf:

BBFILES_DYNAMIC += " \
    qt5-layer:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/qt5-layer/*/*/*.bb \
    qt5-layer:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/qt5-layer/*/*/*.bbappend \
    openembedded-layer:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/openembedded-layer/*/*/*.bb \
    openembedded-layer:${LAYERDIR}/dynamic-layers/openembedded-layer/*/*/*.bbappend \
"

3. Find the right collection names. Don’t guess: read them from the other layer’s layer.conf:

grep BBFILE_COLLECTIONS ../meta-openembedded/*/conf/layer.conf

4. Verify it works with and without the optional layer:

# Is the optional layer in the build?
bitbake-layers show-layers

# Are my appends actually applied?
bitbake-layers show-appends | grep -A3 qtbase

# Does my new recipe exist?
bitbake-layers show-recipes my-tool

Then remove the optional layer from bblayers.conf (bitbake-layers remove-layer ...) and parse again. The build should still work, and your dynamic recipes and appends should silently disappear.

Tips and gotchas

  • Use collection names, not directory names. meta-qt5 registers qt5-layer; meta-oe registers openembedded-layer; NXP’s meta-imx-bsp registers fsl-bsp-release. A typo here fails silently: the files just never get parsed. That’s why the verification step above matters.
  • Keep FILESEXTRAPATHS relative to the append. FILESEXTRAPATHS:prepend := "${THISDIR}/${PN}:" works the same inside a dynamic layer. Put patches and service files next to the bbappend, as meta-raspberrypi does for lirc/lircd.service.
  • Always add a machine override (:rpi, :mymachine, …) to appends that change shared recipes. The dynamic layer controls whether the file is parsed; the override controls which builds it affects. Without it, your BSP tweaks leak into every other machine built from the same tree.
  • Don’t hide hard dependencies here. If your board can’t boot without a layer, put it in LAYERDEPENDS. Dynamic layers are for optional integration only.
  • Match the directory depth to your globs. */*/*.bb expects exactly recipes-xxx/name/file.bb. A file one level deeper or shallower is silently ignored.

Conclusion

Dynamic layers solve a real problem in a small amount of configuration. A BSP or product layer can integrate deeply with the wider OpenEmbedded ecosystem without forcing that ecosystem on every user. The recipe for doing it well, from both meta-raspberrypi and meta-summit-som, is short:

  1. Keep LAYERDEPENDS minimal.
  2. Put each optional integration under its own dynamic-layers/ sub-directory, ideally named after the collection that activates it.
  3. Register it in BBFILES_DYNAMIC.
  4. Combine it with machine (and SoC) overrides so the changes only hit your hardware.

Next time you browse a BSP layer, open its layer.conf first. The BBFILES_DYNAMIC block tells you a lot about which parts of the ecosystem it was built to play with.

References

  • meta-raspberrypi: dynamic-layers directory
  • meta-raspberrypi: conf/layer.conf
  • meta-summit-som: dynamic-layers (wrynose-summit-7.2.0.x)
  • meta-summit-som: i.MX kernel recipes
  • Yocto Project Reference Manual: BBFILES_DYNAMIC
  • BitBake User Manual: BBFILES_DYNAMIC (including the ! form)
entry.summary: How BBFILES_DYNAMIC lets a Yocto layer ship optional recipes and bbappends that only activate when another layer is present, explained through meta-raspberrypi and a real i.MX95 BSP.

entry.title: Neural Network Implementation on FPGA using HLS

link.title: Neural Network Implementation on FPGA using HLS

entry.content:
